strengths: The paper identifies a useful distinction: deterministic prediction from pixels does not eliminate confounding between selected, interpretable macro-level features and model outputs. This perspective has a clear audience in explainable AI and causal discovery.

PAGs are an appropriate representation for the proposed analysis, and the background knowledge that predictions cannot cause input features is well motivated. Applying established FCI methodology is a legitimate contribution for this objective.

The exposition is generally accessible. Sections 7.2–7.3 acknowledge important limitations involving partial identification, annotation availability, deterministic feature relationships, and measurement error.
The synthetic example, two image applications, bootstrap analyses, and alternative discovery algorithm provide concrete illustrations of the proposed workflow.
weaknesses: Necessary—address selection in the X-ray experiment. Section 6.1 selects 120 pneumonia images and 120 controls specifically with 'no findings.' Inclusion therefore depends on disease and the explanatory findings, making the dismissal of selection bias in Section 3 unjustified for this application. Selection can alter conditional independences and invalidate the stated causal interpretation of graph endpoints. The sampling mechanism needs to be addressed, or the medical conclusions substantially narrowed.

Necessary—align conclusions with what the graphs identify. Section 6.3 combines directed and partially directed edges into one stability measure, while Figures 9–10 and Section 6.4 sometimes describe features as likely causes or causally irrelevant. A stable possible-cause edge can remain compatible with pure confounding. Conversely, absence of an edge to the prediction does not exclude an indirect causal path; Cardiomegaly in Figure 10 illustrates this concern. Report definite, possible, and confounded relationships separately, examine ancestry before making negative causal claims, and retain bootstrap frequencies as descriptive stability measures.

Necessary—establish the reliability of the empirical independence tests. Chi-square tests can encounter sparse contingency tables with only 240 X-rays, and with 26 multilevel bird attributes and conditioning sets containing up to four variables. The manuscript does not report expected-cell diagnostics or how unreliable tests are handled. Clarify which data splits enter discovery and provide appropriate diagnostics or sensitivity checks. The substantial change from Wing Shape/Wing Pattern under FCI to Crown Color/Size under GRaSP-FCI also warrants more cautious substantive conclusions; clinical or ornithological plausibility does not validate causal recovery.

Necessary—repair the Shapley counterexample in Example 1 and Appendix A. The purported valid-adjustment calculations use marginal substitutions such as E[f'(Z1,z2,Z3)], leaving Z1's distribution unchanged although Z2 causes Z1 in the stated SCM. These are not generally the corresponding macro-level do-intervention expectations. Appendix A.2 also retains a fixed z3 despite declaring Z3 unobserved, without specifying an observable-data estimator that produces those expressions. Define the attribution value function and intervention semantics consistently, then rederive or remove the example. A zero local Shapley attribution also does not itself imply absence of population-level causal relevance.

Optional—strengthen comparative evaluation with an associational baseline using the same macro-level annotations and repeated synthetic trials with known causal structure. The selected LIME/SHAP examples primarily illustrate differences in representation and local versus population-level objectives; they do not isolate the benefit of confounding-aware discovery. Such additions would strengthen the paper, but a new method or state-of-the-art predictive performance is unnecessary for acceptance.
